title: Would You Host a Piece of an AI Data Center in Your Garage?
hook: Instead of building one giant data center, a solar and home-battery company wants to pay homeowners to host small AI compute units — turning thousands of houses into one distributed data center.
key_points: The Verge reports Sunrun, a solar and home-energy-storage company, is piloting 'distributed AI compute.'
Instead of one large facility, it places numerous small compute nodes inside participating homes.
Homeowners are paid to host the hardware, similar to how some already host solar or battery equipment.
It's a genuinely different approach to AI's data-center footprint — spreading it out instead of concentrating it in one place.
content_html: Every AI data center story so far has been about one big building — its land, its power draw, its water, and the neighbors pushing back. The Verge reports a different approach: Sunrun, a solar and home-energy-storage company, is piloting "distributed AI compute," which places numerous small compute units inside participating homes rather than building a single large facility.
extra_html: The pitch to homeowners is straightforward, similar to how some already get paid to host solar panels or home batteries: let a small compute node sit in your garage or utility closet, and get compensated for it. For a company already in the home-energy business, it's a natural extension — pairing your existing home battery and solar setup with a bit of AI compute demand. Whether this scales to matter much for the broader AI data-center footprint is an open question, but it's a genuinely different answer to a problem the industry has mostly tried to solve by building bigger: instead of concentrating AI's power and space needs in one place a community can organize against, spread it thin enough that no single site draws attention.

related.title: Communities Are Pushing Back on AI Data Centers
related.hook: The warehouses that power AI need land, power, and water — and neighbors are starting to say no. New York just signed the nation's first statewide data center ban into law.

related.title: A Fix for AI's Power Crunch: Flexible Data Centers
related.hook: AI's data centers are straining electric grids. One promising fix: build them to flex — easing off power when the grid is stressed, in exchange for getting connected far sooner.

flashcards.prompt: How is Sunrun's 'distributed AI compute' pilot different from a typical AI data center?

choices.text: It spreads small compute units across many homes instead of one large facility
It uses no electricity at all
It only operates inside Sunrun's own corporate offices

flashcards.explanation_html: Rather than one massive building, the model places numerous small compute nodes inside participating homes — spreading the footprint out, not concentrating it.

flashcards.prompt: Why might a company try this instead of building a traditional data center?
flashcards.back_html: Traditional data centers face land, power-grid, and community pushback (see the data center backlash) — a distributed model sidesteps some of that friction.
